learningObjective: Distinguish correct claims about MoE compute/parameter efficiency and imbalance from common misconceptions.

canonicalClaims.claim: In top-k MoE with E experts and k << E, total parameter count scales as O(E) but activated compute per token stays at O(k) plus an O(E) gating term; this decoupling is the source of MoE's parameter-per-flop leverage.
conditions: Router cost is small relative to MLP compute.
nonImplications: Does not imply MoE always outperforms dense; imbalance and communication overheads can absorb the win.

canonicalClaims.claim: MoE serving suffers from routing skew; hot experts bottleneck the batched matmul, and capacity limits or load-balancing losses are used to mitigate this.
conditions: Serving with fixed capacity per expert.
nonImplications: Does not imply imbalance is unavoidable; auxiliary losses reduce it in training.

misconceptions.claim: MoE compute per token scales linearly with E.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Only k out of E experts are activated; the router adds O(E), MLP compute stays O(k).

misconceptions.claim: Expert parallelism cannot help MoE inference.
misconceptions.whyWrong: EP distributes both parameter storage and per-token weight bandwidth across devices.

misconceptions.claim: MoE routing is deterministic and always balanced.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Routing has empirical skew; balancing is an active mitigation.

implementationFacts: Auxiliary balancing loss encourages uniform routing during training.
In serving, capacity factor > 1 (typically 1.25-2) allows some slack before dropping.
performanceScenarios: Mixtral 8x7B uses 8 experts with top-2 routing; parameter count ~47B but active flops per token similar to a 13B dense model.
